items.title: Brazil's Lula wins electoral court challenge against Meta for alleged pro-Bolsonaro algorithm bias
items.description: A judge of Brazil’s top electoral court ruled on Thursday that Meta must adopt measures to immediately secure equal treatment of the two presidential candidates ahead of an Oct. 25 runoff.

items._ogDesc: A judge of Brazil’s top electoral court ruled on Thursday that Meta must adopt measures to immediately secure equal treatment of the two presidential candidates ahead of an Oct. 25 runoff.
items.body:
SAO PAULO — A judge of Brazil’s top electoral court ruled on Thursday that Meta must adopt measures to immediately secure equal treatment of the two presidential candidates ahead of an Oct. 25 runoff.

The ruling comes shortly after Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is running against Flávio Bolsonaro, filed a complaint that accused the tech company that owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favour opposition candidate Bolsonaro ahead of the election.

Justice Marco Aurélio Bellizze ruled Meta cannot reduce the distribution of political content, restrict searches or remove posts in a way that creates an imbalance between Lula and Bolsonaro. His ruling also orders the company to ensure its artificial intelligence tool applies identical criteria to both candidacies.

Bellizze said in his ruling that Meta must pay a fine of 500,000 reais (US$98,000) per day if it fails to comply.

The legal filing of the Lula campaign, to which The Associated Press had access, said Meta has subjected Lula’s campaign materials and organic posts to “unjustified reductions in reach.” It also said Meta has not complied with a plan submitted to the electoral court to address these issues.

Meta declined to comment on the ruling.

Lula’s campaign argues that accounts and advertisements associated with Flávio Bolsonaro have reportedly received artificially inflated visibility, with engagement metrics rivaling global celebrities. The two are in a close race for the presidency, after the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro garnered 47 per cent of the vote against 45 per cent of the incumbent in the first round on Oct. 4.

Lula’s complaint also claims there’s a stark disparity in Meta’s artificial intelligence tools, with users failing to generate campaign images related to the 80-year-old president via WhatsApp’s “Meta AI” feature, but being able to do so if they want to promote content in support of Flávio Bolsonaro.

Gean Ferreira and Evelyn Santos, both lawyers for the Lula campaign, said in a statement that Meta’s content delivery is selective against the incumbent and favourable to Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump.

“On one hand, content from candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his supporters faces delivery restrictions, without any justification or transparency,” the lawyers said. ”On the other hand, profiles acting as political operatives for the opposing side ... receive a disproportionate and artificial reach, garnering more views even than global celebrities.”

Lula’s campaign wants Brazil’s top electoral court to order an immediate end to the content restrictions and pressure Meta to make up for the lost traction by doubling its reach to rectify the harm inflicted.

On Oct. 11, as Lula’s voters started complaining about their use of Meta tools, the big tech company told the electoral court it rejects accusations of being skewed to Bolsonaro. The company admitted it has faced technical glitches that affect accounts beyond Brazil. It also said it acts in full compliance with Brazil’s electoral regulations and is committed to providing equal platform access for all political parties.

Mauricio Savarese, The Associated Press

items.title: SeatGeek Canada hit with more fines totalling $22,500 over ticket resale violations
items.description: SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.

items._ogDesc: SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.
items.body:
TORONTO — SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.

The province’s consumer beware website shows the new fines issued to the ticket resale platform earlier this month total $22,500 collectively.

The website says the first of the two fines amounts to $15,000 and is for allegedly making a ticket available for sale or facilitating a sale of a seat beyond the resale price limit.

The second fine is for $7,500 and is for allegedly failing to disclose the total price of a ticket when a seat was purchased from a primary seller.

  • Latest updates on company news here

SeatGeek Canada did not answer questions about what events the fines stem from or whether it will fight the penalties.

“We are doing our best to comply but we have yet to receive meaningful direction from the government on how to do so,” spokesperson Cameron Papp said Thursday in an email.

Giulia Paikin, a spokesperson for the Ontario Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery Stephen Crawford, also did not answer questions about the nature of the penalties.

However, she sent a statement that repeated nearly verbatim what the province has previously said about anyone responsible for price cap violations facing fines of up to $250,000.

“We will not hesitate to hold bad actors who break the rules accountable,” an email from Paikin said.

SeatGeek’s new fines stem from legislation the province implemented earlier this year, after fans complained about resale prices for tickets to Taylor Swift’s Eras tour in 2024 and last year’s playoff run by the Toronto Blue Jays.

The legislation was meant to keep people from reselling seats to Ontario events for well beyond face value and tamp down on scalpers profiting off their ability to scoop up tickets to hot concerts and shows.

After the legislation came into effect, the province issued $25,000 in fines to SeatGeek in August for similar offences.

A $20,000 fine for fellow resale website StubHub Canada followed in September.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

When SeatGeek was given its first round of fines, it told The Canadian Press it had notified third-party sellers on its platform about the new law but was still seeking guidance from the province around how to comply with the regulations.

The platform argued it is challenging to confirm the original value of tickets because many sellers don’t have access to that information. Sometimes seats have changed hands several times before they wind up on a resale site and if tickets were bought as part of a broader package, like a season’s seat arrangement, it can be hard to break down the value of a single ticket.

To address these issues, SeatGeek said it has asked Ontario to define what counts as acceptable proof of a ticket’s original price and for guidance around how a marketplace is expected to validate the cost of seats.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: The CEO of Cleveland-Cliffs said the company’s decision to issue hundreds of layoff notices at the Stelco plant in Hamilton, Ont., was a 'business decision to concentrate production.'
items.body:
The CEO of Cleveland-Cliffs said the company’s decision to issue hundreds of layoff notices at the Stelco plant in Hamilton, Ont., was a “business decision to concentrate production.”

In an exclusive interview with BNN Bloomberg Thursday, Lourenco Goncalves said he intends to rehire the laid off workers, calling the job cuts “temporary.”

“Stelco is having a great year, we are making money, the Canadian market continues to react positively to things that we are doing,” he said.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

The federal government said Cleveland-Cliffs, who bought Stelco in 2024, made a pledge to protect jobs. But last month, the U.S. company announced it was shutting down part of its Hamilton operation and cutting up to 500 jobs due to U.S. tariffs put on Canada by the Trump administration.

Ottawa said the move breaks the commitments made under the Investment Canada Act.

Industry Minister Melanie Joly said “everything is on the table” on Wednesday, including a forced divestment of assets or financial penalties if it does not heed the federal government’s warnings to stop the cuts.

Goncalves called Joly’s comments “bullying and harassment.”

“We are not in Canada to lay off people, we believe in the workforce, we believe in the market, we believe that Canada is a country of laws,” he said, comparing any potential action by the federal government to when former Venezuelan president Hugo Chavez nationalized the steel industry in 2008.

“I don’t think that Canada is Venezuela, let alone Venezuela under Hugo Chavez.”

Goncalves said his company is prepared to go to court to defend their position and that they had not violated the deal they made with former industry minister Francois-Philippe Champagne.

Goncalves said that Champagne “rolled the red carpet for us” when Cleveland-Cliffs was orchestrating their purchase of Stelco.

“We did not expect less than two years after we acquired the company to be treated like a pariah,” he said.

“If that’s what Canada will do to attract foreign investment into Canada, I don’t believe that they will be very successful.”

items._ogDesc: Cultural sector groups say they’re starting to worry about the Liberal government’s silence on $600 million in promised funding.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Cultural sector groups say they’re starting to worry about the Liberal government’s silence on $600 million in promised funding.

“Funding that was supposed to reduce uncertainty is actually now leading to greater uncertainty, because we don’t know when it’s going to materialize,” said Reynolds Mastin, president and CEO of the Canadian Media Producers Association.

“It’s critical that it be delivered as soon as possible.”

The Liberal government introduced the Online Streaming Act in 2023 to bring streaming companies into the system that requires cable companies and broadcasters to contribute to or broadcast Canadian content. The funding from traditional players has diminished as Canadians have moved to streaming platforms.

In 2024, the CRTC made an initial order under the Online Streaming Act requiring large streaming companies like Netflix to pay five per cent of their annual Canadian revenues to funds devoted to producing Canadian content, including local TV news. In May, it increased that requirement to 15 per cent.

In June, the federal government changed course. It told the CRTC to review the recent decision to regulate online streamers and said the government would instead provide funding directly to Canadian content producers. Those financial contributions from streamers were already on hold because of an ongoing court challenge.

While the government cited affordability for consumers as the main reason for the move, Culture Minister Marc Miller also said at the time the industry was suffering while money for Canadian content was frozen by litigation.

Four months later, the government still isn’t saying when it will provide the new direction to the CRTC or disburse the $600 million. That has left the sector without either payments from streamers or the promised government funding.

Hélène Messier, president and CEO of the Association québécoise de la production médiatique, said the government described the situation as urgent back in June.

“And it is urgent. The situation in the audiovisual industry is very bad,” she said, noting a significant decrease in the volume of production in recent years.

“We want to know where we stand.”

Canadian content contributions and rules for streamers became a flashpoint in trade talks with the United States over the summer.

“[Prime Minister Mark Carney] said that culture and French language was so important that it was one of the reasons why they ended the negotiation with the Americans,” Messier said.

“So now I think they have to act accordingly. If it is important, then do something.”

It’s not clear what exactly was at issue during the trade talks. Carney pointed to the visibility of Canadian content on streaming services, while U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said the issue for the U.S. is streaming companies having to make financial contribution toward Canadian content.

The Online Streaming Act says streamers should ensure “discoverability” of Canadian programs, including French language content.

A spokesperson for the culture minister declined to answer when asked when the new policy direction and the $600 million will be released. The spokesperson also did not answer when asked whether the new policy direction to the CRTC is on hold until there is a trade agreement with the U.S.

Reynolds said he’s getting phone calls almost daily from producers asking about the status of the government funding.

“A number of shows were waiting for that funding to materialize months ago, and they’re still waiting,” he said.

Messier said the delay will make it more difficult to spend the money this fiscal year.

“You cannot do a production tomorrow morning. It’s a long process to be able to spend the money wisely,” she said.

Reynolds said a show takes months of planning between getting the green light and going into production.

“Studio space has to be secured. Locations... the cast has to secured,” he said. “The longer the delay, the longer it is before new shows actually get produced, let alone make it onto screens in Canada and around the world.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

items.title: Supreme Court hears challenge of law clearing path for Ontario Place redevelopment
items.description: The Supreme Court of Canada heard arguments Thursday from a coalition challenging the constitutionality of legislation that clears the way for major changes at Ontario Place.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Construction is seen at Ontario Place in Toronto, Tuesday, June 24, 2025. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Chris Young]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Chris Young</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The Supreme Court of Canada heard arguments Thursday from a coalition challenging the constitutionality of legislation that clears the way for major changes at Ontario Place.
items.body:
The Supreme Court of Canada heard arguments Thursday from a coalition challenging the constitutionality of legislation that clears the way for major changes at Ontario Place.

Judges on the top court peppered counsel for the coalition and the Crown with questions and comments about their respective legal positions before reserving the court’s decision until a later date.

The case unfolding in the Supreme Court could reverberate far beyond the Toronto waterfront park that opened in 1971.

Over the years, Ontario Place has featured a spherical theatre that showed movies on a huge screen, children’s play areas, a revolving concert stage and several pavilions suspended above the water.

The provincial government wants to redevelop the theme park to include an elaborate spa operated by a private company, a relocated Ontario Science Centre, revamped play and shoreline areas, a parking facility and a provincial police detachment.

The coalition Ontario Place Protectors challenged the province’s Rebuilding Ontario Place Act, arguing that it insulates state action from scrutiny by the courts and therefore violates the Constitution.

The coalition also argued that exemptions from environmental and heritage laws and municipal noise regulations amount to a breach of public trust.

An Ontario judge dismissed the application in 2024 and a challenge of the ruling in the provincial Court of Appeal was also unsuccessful.

Writing on behalf of a unanimous Court of Appeal, Justice Grant Huscroft said there’s no doubt the provincial government’s decision to redevelop Ontario Place is strongly opposed by a number of concerned citizens and organizations.

Political opposition to the plan has not swayed the government and the coalition has turned to the court in an effort to stop it, Huscroft said.

“But there is no basis for the court to do so. The court is not an alternative forum for resolving political grievances. The only legitimate question for the court is whether the impugned provisions of ROPA violate the law or the Constitution,” he said.

“They do not, and the appeal must be dismissed.”

In January, the Supreme Court agreed to hear the Ontario Place Protectors’ case.

The coalition says provincial superior courts have historical and inherent jurisdiction to review laws and government actions protected under section 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867, and to provide effective remedies when governments do not respect the limits on their powers.

The coalition says the Rebuilding Ontario Place Act’s scope is unprecedented and it appears to violate section 96 by removing the essential core powers of the courts.

It argues the legislation severely limits or eliminates the ability of courts to hold Crown officials accountable through declaratory actions, damage awards and injunctions when they have acted beyond their powers.

The coalition is also seeking to have the doctrine of public trust acknowledged as an unwritten constitutional principle rooted in English common law and inherited by Canada.

It argues the doctrine of public trust maintains that natural and cultural assets are essential to public welfare and must be safeguarded by the state in its role as trustee.

Margie Zeidler, the daughter of Ontario Place architect Eberhard Zeidler, remembers visiting the park as a child.

“It was extraordinary. It was a public place,” she said in an interview. “You could have a picnic in the forest. You could watch films at Cinesphere. You could watch any musical performance at the forum.”

Zeidler, a member of the Ontario Place Protectors coalition, said the provincial government’s actions have made the fight about more than just the historic theme park.

“It became more, not about Ontario Place, but about, wait a minute, what democracy are we living in here?” she said. “I didn’t know governments could do that.”

In their written submission to the Supreme Court, the Crown and the Ontario attorney general say the case should be dismissed.

The immunity provided by the provincial legislation does not go as far as the coalition alleges, the submission says: “(The act) does not make Ontario Place a lawless zone.”

Rather, it immunizes the Crown, its servants and agents from civil causes of action arising from specific circumstances, the submission says.

The Crown and attorney general are also urging the court to reject the claim that the legislation is invalid because of the doctrine of public trust.

“The novel doctrine articulated by the Appellant is not an unwritten constitutional principle, and even if such a doctrine existed in law, which is denied, there is no evidence in the record that could warrant applying this far-reaching new doctrine to Ontario Place,” the submission says.

The case has attracted submissions from interveners, including the federal attorney general, several provinces, First Nations, civil liberties groups and environmental organizations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

items.title: Eight U.S. states are suing OpenAI, saying it’s hurting kids and lying to adults
items.description: At least eight states are suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Attendees gather at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in San Francisco. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jeff Chiu</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: At least eight states are suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults.
items.body:
HARRISBURG, Pa. — At least eight U.S. states are suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI, saying the company’s popular chatbot model violated state consumer protection laws by hurting children and deceiving adults in what prosecutors described as a reckless pursuit of profit.

The company’s chatbot model, ChatGPT, is giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to commit suicide or hurt or kill others, the lawsuits said.

At the same time, the lawsuits allege that chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable and on teenagers, the first generation to grow up with artificial intelligence.

“OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement.

The states also accused OpenAI of giving life to rogue AI models -- or “cyberhacking agents” as one lawsuit called them -- that hacked into other companies, lied to human users and wrote themselves new mission instructions.

In a statement, San Francisco-based OpenAI said it has built safety protections into ChatGPT for children, and that it would continue to do so to improve the model. It also said it is reviewing what it calls “misaligned models” and that it had found nothing close to the rogue incident discovered in July when an AI agent hacked into another AI company.

Co-ordinated lawsuits gain traction

The wave of lawsuits is the latest filed by states under their consumer protection laws, accusing tech giants that offer AI chatbots and social media platforms of harming children. The states that filed separate lawsuits Wednesday in state courts are Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia.

Matthew Bergman, the founding attorney of the Social Media Victims Law Center, called the lawsuits “the most significant coordinated state action ever taken against an artificial intelligence company.”

In its lawsuit, Arizona said ChatGPT encourages teens to share personal information with it and, at times, discourages them from sharing that information with parents, authorities or friends.

The states say that the risks and harms -- to teenagers and to the broader public from rogue agents -- were foreseeable, but that OpenAI has misled people into thinking that ChatGPT undergoes adequate safety testing while the company undermines safety in the pursuit of profit.

“Those revenues have come at great cost to the public, which has suffered irreparable harm -- including lost loved ones, disturbing cyberattacks, and now a plausible threat of civilizational collapse -- due to (OpenAI’s) reckless behavior and ChatGPT’s uniquely dangerous features and content,” Idaho wrote in its lawsuit.

ChatGPT is the most popular chatbot in the world, commanding nearly half the American marketplace, states said in their lawsuits.

The AI landscape is evolving

It’s possible all of the allegations in the states’ lengthy lawsuits date to incidents and findings before August, when OpenAI introduced a version of ChatGPT designed for teenagers, with stronger protections around subjects like suicide and sexual chats.

Still, the states said it is far from clear that the current version is any less dangerous.

A watchdog group, Common Sense Media, said last week that some of OpenAI’s protections in its ChatGPT for Teens product don’t work as intended and it urged OpenAI to restrict the chatbot to adults until it can offer a safe product for teens.

Co-ordinated, multistate lawsuits against the tech industry have borne fruit.

In August, Meta agreed to add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in an US$18-billion landmark legal settlement that ended a trial over teen social media addiction and settled claims filed by nearly every state.

Although the safety measures that Meta agreed to adopt did not apply industrywide, the company quickly urged its competitors to adopt similar measures.

OpenAI is making a similar appeal.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company is committed to working with states on “advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry -- not just one company.”

ChatGPT is intended for users age 13 and older, and users under 18 need permission from a parent or guardian to use it, OpenAI said. The chatbot model for teens is designed to reduce exposure to self-harm, violence, eating disorders and explicit sexual or graphic content, it said.

Nearly nine in 10 teens who use ChatGPT use it for learning, information, skill-building or productivity, the company said. On average, teens spend under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT, it said.

It also said it works with external experts who review policies and the model’s behaviour.

Marc Levy, The Associated Press

items.title: Data centre for Canada’s cyber spy agency to be built in Ottawa area
items.description: The federal government is looking to build a data centre in the national capital region to support Canada's cyber spy agency, saying it will focus on the “mid to long-term objectives” of government operations, security and technology.
items._ogDesc: The federal government is looking to build a data centre in the national capital region to support Canada's cyber spy agency, saying it will focus on the “mid to long-term objectives” of government operations, security and technology.
items.body:
The federal government is looking to build a data centre in the national capital region to support Canada’s cyber spy agency, saying it will focus on the “mid to long-term objectives” of government operations, security and technology.

Defence Construction Canada issued an advance procurement notice for the data centre last week, saying it is informing “design-builders of an upcoming contract located” in the Ottawa area.

The estimated cost of the project is $1.5 billion to $1.8 billion, with the tender expected to be issued in 2027.

“To increase its capacity in supporting the mid to long-term objectives related to operations, security, and technology modernization, the Government of Canada is planning to design and construction a data centre facility within the national capital region,” said the notice issued on the federal government’s website.

“This data center of 60 MW will enable the onboarding of next-generation capabilities with tailored mechanical and electrical configurations to meet distinct technology requirements throughout the facility.”

The Communications Security Establishment Canada (CSE) says the proposed data centre would provide “additional secure computing capacity” to support its “current and future operational requirements.”

“It is part of the Government of Canada’s broader defence investments, including investments through CSE to modernize the secure infrastructure and capabilities needed to respond to evolving threats and support Canada’s national security and defence priorities,” CSE said in a statement to CTV News Ottawa.

“Project planning and site selection activities remain ongoing. Additional information will be shared as decisions are finalized and appropriate to disclose. To protect national security and the integrity of its operations, CSE does not disclose specific operational or technical requirements beyond what is publicly available.”

The federal government launched Canada’s Responsible Data Centre Development Principles in September, outlining how Canada builds the data centre capacity it needs.

According to the government, the principles “sets five clear expectations” for data centre projects:

  • Data centres must create lasting local benefits.
  • Data centres must not shift electricity costs to Canadians.
  • Data centres must minimize water use and environmental impacts.
  • Data centres must be transparent about local impacts.
  • Data centres must bring strategic value to Canada.

The government’s proposed data centre facility for CSE would include a “small office space and a shipping and receiving area,” according to the notice. It also notes the federal government has not approved proceeding with the new data centre at this time.

Data centres have “tremendous appetite for power”

In August, Ottawa city council passed a motion directing city staff to develop a framework for assessing data centre proposals. The study will look at assessing data centres based on their size and impact, including environmental and industrial standards, community benefits and possible amendments to the official plan.

Hydro Ottawa’s CEO Bryce Conrad told council in June that the utility had received 34 requests in the past two years for “large load customers,” which would require nearly 90 per cent of the average amount of power used by the City of Ottawa in 2025.

“These are prospective customers who need a significant amount of electricity, think of government, national defence, hospitals, university campuses, and yes, data centres,” Conrad said, noting data centres accounted for 653 megawatts of the 1,075 megawatts requested to Hydro Ottawa.

“It’s no secret that there’s a lot of tension these days around data centres, AI technologies, and their tremendous appetite for power.”

During an interview with Newstalk 580 CFRA in August, Conrad said Hydro Ottawa is working to build capacity to meet the demand for data centres and large-load customers.

“We’re probably being asked to build in the next two or three years, that which has taken us about 110 years to build.”

items.title: CNN, Axios and other publishers join Google’s AI news program
items.description: Skydance’s, the Financial Times, Axios and other publishers joined Google’s news program to license their content for generative AI features.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[FILE - The CNN logo is displayed at the entrance to the CNN Center in Atlanta on Feb. 2, 2022. (AP Photo/Ron Harris, File)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Skydance’s, the Financial Times, Axios and other publishers joined Google’s news program to license their content for generative AI features.
items.body:
Skydance’s, the Financial Times, Axios and other publishers joined Google’s news program to license their content for generative AI features and explore ways to drive audience engagement.

The search-engine giant said on Thursday that the program, which started as a pilot last year with partners like The Washington Post, now includes more than 400 publications globally.

The deal marks CNN’s first partnership since Paramount Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, as CEO David Ellison seeks to position the combined company as a technology-driven media business.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

As part of these agreements, publishers will provide enhanced content rights, allowing Google to develop new AI features, while Google will pay participating news organizations for their content. Financial terms were not disclosed.

“Google’s innovation with generative AI has changed how people discover information and content, and now those tools will help us explore new ways to discover and engage audiences,” said Sam Felix, CNN’s senior vice president of strategic partnerships and business development.

Google said the AI features will come with clear attribution and direct links, helping readers to connect with the sources they value.

The announcement comes at a time when publishers are stepping up legal efforts to prevent AI companies from using their content without permission to train large language models.

  • Latest updates on company news here

News publishers are also grappling with declining referral traffic as search engines roll out AI-generated answers that allow users to consume information without clicking through to websites.

CNN said the deal is in line with its strategy to protect its intellectual property, adding that it has multiple commercial partnerships and ongoing discussions with other industry players.

The network operates television, streaming and digital news services worldwide, including CNN International and CNN Originals, as well as a direct-to-consumer subscription service and CNN Newsource.

items._ogDesc: Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is defending his decision to change his stance on when data centres might be considered for approval to operate in the province.
items.body:
HALIFAX — Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is defending his decision to change his stance on when data centres might be considered for approval to operate in the province.

In June, the premier said it was too soon to turn his government’s attention to the matter, and that it would not be discussed until far into the future.

A few months later, he softened that stance, opening a door to consider proposals from the sector.

“A lot has happened … in the world, geopolitics, all kinds of situations there,” Houston told reporters Thursday.

“When you look at some of the positioning of the federal government around data sovereignty, around the regulations that would be required, (they) definitely were thoughtful and had an impact on me.”

The premier had previously said discussions about data centres would have to wait until the province had completed major energy generation projects, including the ambitious Wind West offshore wind farms.

“We’re going to generate significant amounts of energy … (and) at that point in time, that would be a more appropriate discussion,” he said on June 18.

At the time, the premier said the discussion about data centres “is so far out in the future … but there wouldn’t be a commitment to a data centre unless we could fully supply the energy without any risk to Nova Scotians.”

Late last month, however, Houston said data centres are becoming increasingly critical pieces of infrastructure, adding that Canada can’t rely on other countries to store its data. He said he became more open to considering data centre proposals after Ottawa rolled out its new rules.

“I think the sentiment of that (June) statement was that we wouldn’t allow an impact on ratepayers,” Houston said Thursday. “We’re not going to drive up the rates to let another user, any type of industrial use, have their power while households and Nova Scotians pay more. That sentiment remains.”

Data centres, used in AI and other high-tech industries, are typically massive operations that require immense amounts of electricity to run and cool off computer servers.

EverWind Fuels, the company planning a large-scale green hydrogen project in Cape Breton to be powered by onshore wind, says it’s exploring setting up a data centre at an existing industrial site at Point Tupper, N.S.

The proposed data centre “would form part of the broader Point Tupper Energy Hub and complement EverWind’s clean energy projects across Nova Scotia,” company spokesperson Claire Parsons said in an email Thursday.

Parsons declined to say if the proposed data centre would be used for artificial intelligence.

Official Opposition Leader Claudia Chender called Houston’s changed stance on data centres a “stunning reversal.”

“When the premier said not long ago that we were not considering AI data centres, not today, not tomorrow … people took him at his word as they watched these debates play out in other places,” Chender, the NDP leader, told reporters Thursday.

Last month, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew rejected plans for a massive AI data centre southeast of Winnipeg. Kinew said the project’s size, energy use and community impact outweighed its limited gains. He said he was also skeptical of the long-term demand for centres of this scale given advances in computing.

Meanwhile, Bell Canada intends to quadruple the size of its planned data centre project in Saskatchewan, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying last month the project is expected to bring in more than $50 billion in capital investment.

Alberta has also embraced data centre development. Electricity generator TransAlta Corp. announced plans in February to power a new data centre west of Edmonton. This came after the provincial technology minister said in 2024 that province was hoping to see $100 billion worth of artificial intelligence data centres under construction over five years.

Environmental advocates have raised concerns about the massive volume of energy and water used by data centres. They’ve also warned about the potential for chemical pollution.

A recent United Nations University report says the environmental footprint of data centres globally already rivals some of the world’s largest countries. The report also predicts their water and energy use and pollution will double in just four years as use of artificial intelligence grows.

Chender and interim Liberal leader Iain Rankin both said Thursday they have serious concerns about the potential environmental impacts and water use tied to a data centre.

Houston said Thursday a data centre in Nova Scotia would have to go through an approval process that could exceed federal requirements. This means the process would need to consider the impact on the environment and ratepayers.

Both opposition leaders said these protections should be built into legislation.

“It’s one thing to say that water and environmental concerns and ratepayers will be protected, but it’s not a fact that the premier’s word is stronger than regulations or legislation,” Rankin said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Lyndsay Armstrong, The Canadian Press

items.title: What persistently high bond yields could mean for the commercial mortgage market
items.description: Avison Young flags cap rate pressure as lenders tighten underwriting on income properties
items.content: <p>Avison Young flags cap rate pressure as lenders tighten underwriting on income properties</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639276802996438662.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Avison Young flags cap rate pressure as lenders tighten underwriting on income properties
items.body:
Persistently high long-term bond yields are shaping up as the deciding variable for Canada’s commercial mortgage market, with Avison Young warning that capitalization rates may struggle to hold if borrowing costs stay elevated into 2027.

In its Q3 2026 Canadian cap rate and investment trends report, the real estate services firm said yields no longer move on central bank policy alone, with persistent inflation, government borrowing, trade disruptions, energy markets and geopolitical tension lifting financing costs and investors’ required returns.

The cap rate, a property’s net operating income divided by its value, is where that pressure lands. Higher cap rates mean lower valuations and smaller loans for income-property clients.

National benchmarks sat at 4.55% for high-density urban multifamily, 5.85% for new single-tenant industrial and 6.90% for downtown class A office in the third quarter, following a second quarter in which Toronto anchored Canada’s commercial real estate rebound.

The five-year Government of Canada bond yield closed at 3.60% on October 2, up from 3.35% on September 1, according to Bank of Canada data, extending an oil-fuelled bond selloff that pushed Canada’s 10-year yield to 3.9% in September. 

“Bond markets are essentially doing some of the Bank of Canada’s job for them,” RBC economist Carrie Freestone said on the bank’s The 10-Minute Take podcast, as bond yields are already repricing Canada’s fixed mortgage market.

How are lenders pricing commercial mortgage risk?

Credit is still flowing, but on tighter terms. Conventional multifamily loans price 130 to 200 basis points over the five-year Government of Canada yield.

Loans insured by Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) price 55 to 100 basis points over it, the survey said.

Office spreads run 150 to 250 basis points. Multifamily arrears are trending up, and CMHC-insured applications fell from the prior quarter.

“While capital remains available across all asset classes, uncertainty related to geopolitical tensions, trade disruption, and rising bond yields is beginning to reduce borrowing capacity and increase lender caution,” said Ron Dezman, senior vice-president, debt capital and advisory, at Avison Young in Edmonton.

"In the CMHC lending market, underwriting assumptions for rental growth and threshold interest rates are becoming more conservative as supply risk deepens across several markets."

What higher yields mean for brokers’ commercial clients

Private investors made 48% of third-quarter acquisitions worth $5 million or more, according to CoStar data in the report. Mortgage renewal or maturity ranked as the second-most common reason owners sold multifamily assets.

“For multifamily pricing, bond yields will be the dominant story for the remainder of 2026, as a persistence of higher yields will likely place upward pressure on cap rates, especially with the relatively flat near-term income growth expectations,” said Carey Buntain, principal, capital markets, at Avison Young in Vancouver.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, flagged the move at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

“I think rates will probably go up in October. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last sixty to ninety days. Bank of Canada bond rates are up 60 points. Like everything’s been going up already. So it’s just a natural part of the market,” Armstrong said.

items.title: Federal government delivers $100 million to push Wind West project ahead
items.description: The federal government blew into Halifax Thursday morning to announce $100 million to advance offshore wind development in Nova Scotia.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Tim Hodgson, federal minister of environment and natural resources, announces a $100 million dollar plan to help develop offshore wind farms off the coast of Nova Scotia. (Jesse Thomas/CTV Atlantic)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: The federal government blew into Halifax Thursday morning to announce $100 million to advance offshore wind development in Nova Scotia.
items.body:
The federal government blew into Halifax Thursday morning to announce $100 million to advance offshore wind development in Nova Scotia.

Tim Hodgson, the federal minister of energy and natural resources, along with Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston, made the announcement on Thursday morning in Dartmouth, calling the offshore wind project a transformative economic opportunity.

The Atlantic Ocean and the shorelines off Nova Scotia are recognized as having some of the strongest winds in the world and represent a source of abundant clean energy, and something that can be exported from the province and across the country, and even further south into the United States.

The project is referred to as Wind West and, geographically speaking, while it’s located on the East Coast of Canada, the idea is that it will send power and clean energy west, to the rest of Canada.

It’s a Nova Scotia-lead initiative and a key component of the Atlantic Energy Strategy, which was referred to the federal Major Projects office in September 2025 and focusses on developing energy projects that can benefit the Atlantic provinces.

The $100 million announced Thursday will go towards spurring development and securing major investments to move the Wind West project from a concept into development, said Hodgson.

“Nova Scotia’s world-class, wind and highly skilled offshore workforce, developed through the legacy of offshore oil and gas, give Canada a competitive advantage in the potentially $1 trillion global offshore wind market,” he said.

“We will unlock Atlantic Canada’s massive potential by accelerating offshore wind development and strengthening Nova Scotia’s position as a supplier of reliable, affordable and clean energy to customers in the province and across Canada.”

  • Download the CTV News App for breaking news alerts and video on all the top stories

Before the offshore wind turbines can be built, companies who are interested in investing will need reliable data and information about the ocean and wind conditions, said government officials.

That’s why $5 million from the overall funding will go towards the deployment of floating light detection and range finding mounted buoys that can measure offshore wind speeds and detect ocean conditions, that will help prepare for the call for bids, which is expected to go out early in 2027.

The federal government is also providing an additional $3 million to Net Zero Atlantic to expand their existing modelling to include transmission of offshore wind power from Nova Scotia into Quebec, Ontario and beyond, in order to help with transmission cable routing.

Houston, who is also Nova Scotia’s energy minister, said the announcement is a major step forward in making the province a global leader in offshore wind energy development.

“Nova Scotia is no longer at the end of the energy transmission line,” said Houston. “We are the starting point.”

Houston says the collaboration between the provincial and federal governments is allowing them to unlock a generational economic opportunity that will attract investment and create good paying jobs and strengthen the economy.

“We aren’t just protecting our own grid,” said Houston. “We are powering Canada.”

Government officials estimate that over the full lifetime and span of the Wind West project it will help create more than 17,000 jobs.

The majority of the $100 million will go towards the province and federal government for research and sub-sea work to determine the best places to drill boreholes to analyze the seafloor and find the best sites for future wind platforms.

“What we’re doing now is working with the province to determine where those boreholes will be drilled, because that will influence the kind of bids we get back,” said Hodgson, who confirmed that work will be completed over the next year.

Government officials say calls for bids for construction of the offshore leases and the construction of wind turbines will go out to tender in early 2027.

The post Canadian Bond Yields & Borrowing Rates To Rise With US Inflation: BMO appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian bond yields are rising as hot US inflation is driving market expectations of four rate hikes from the Bank of Canada.
items.body:
The cross-border flow of goods is slow, but Canada’s imports of American inflation are ramping up. Government of Canada (GoC) short-term bond yields have climbed sharply since February. Gas prices were behind the initial surge, but yields are still climbing after gas stalled. A new report from BMO Capital Markets attributes the continued rise to hot U.S. inflation. The bank warns that markets are pricing in a full point of rate hikes from the Bank of Canada (BoC) by the end of 2027.

Canadian Bond Yields Pushed Higher By Hot U.S. Inflation

Higher gas prices have driven Canadian bond yields (and inflation) higher since February. BoC Governor Tiff Macklem warned yesterday that “every major central bank is worried…” because “…these costs have to go somewhere,” highlights BMO chief economist Douglas Porter.

Porter’s research shows the GoC 2-year bond yield’s correlation with gas prices at r=0.8, 1.0 being a perfect correlation. Gas prices and bond yields are moving very closely together, with the divergence only starting in September. Gas prices stabilized that month, but Canadian short- and medium-term yields rose further.

Porter flags the strong US jobs report as the catalyst that month. It was followed by a US Federal Reserve speech at Jackson Hole that was hawkish, suggesting the economy is running too hot. American inflation reported yesterday reinforced those concerns, as annual growth hit 3.7% in September, well above the 2% target.

Canadian yields are responding to that pressure, in addition to the energy bump. “Accordingly, the warm U.S. CPI has bumped Canadian yields again, with 2s backing up to 3.25%,” warns Porter.

Markets Expect Canadian Rates Will Rise 1 Point

Canada’s 2-year government bond yield hit 3.25% this week, reflecting expectations of tighter monetary policy. “That’s a full 100 bps above overnight rates, and the market is indeed expecting that much tightening by end-2027,” explains Porter.

The aggressive rise means higher mortgage rates may be ahead. A full point added to the overnight rate would trickle directly into variable rates. Fixed-rate mortgages are driven by bond yields, meaning they’re likely to lead here. BMO questions whether that much tightening is warranted while tariffs and trade uncertainty weigh on Canada. “That seems like a lot,” bluntly states Porter.

BMO Questions Scale of Tightening Amid Weak Economy

The market may be pricing in higher rates, but Canada’s economy may not be able to handle them. “Now, GoC yields are being largely pulled by domestic data—the weak jobs data helped pull them lower—and U.S. yields,” explains Porter.

Porter isn’t dismissing rate hikes, but suggests that market expectations are inflated. Higher rates would throttle demand, reducing inflation further. However, there’s still the matter of currency value that Porter doesn’t address. The situation the BoC faces is a little more complicated than just a demand issue.

Global commodities such as oil, wheat, and corn are generally priced in US dollars. That’s even the case for Canadian oil, which is priced based on global demand. Weak consumption can cool domestic price pressure, but a weaker loonie can still raise import costs. If hot US inflation keeps American rates elevated while Canadian weakness calls for relief, the BoC faces a difficult trade-off. A policy miss could deepen the slowdown or prolong inflation, raising stagflation risks.

items.title: Customer satisfaction with top banks grows – but there’s a catch
items.description: Younger Canadians are eyeing fintechs as fees and rates loosen their loyalty to traditional banks
items.content: <p>Younger Canadians are eyeing fintechs as fees and rates loosen their loyalty to traditional banks</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0321_638766022774937297.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Younger Canadians are eyeing fintechs as fees and rates loosen their loyalty to traditional banks
items.body:
Canadians are slightly happier with their banks this year, but the gain hides a loyalty problem that could reshape where younger borrowers take their business.

Overall customer satisfaction rose 3 points on a 1,000-point scale, lifted mainly by the Big 5 banks, according to the JD Power 2026 Canada Retail Banking Satisfaction Study.

However, fintechs – newer online banks – outscored both the Big 5 and midsize banks on many factors that drive satisfaction, and they are drawing a disproportionate share of younger Canadians planning to move their primary banking relationship.

Among Gen Z and Gen Y customers of traditional retail banks, 17% said they probably or definitely will switch primary banks within 12 months, a five-year high.

Four of the five leading reasons involve product offerings such as fees, interest rates and promotions.

“Younger customers can be satisfied with their bank and still leave if they see a better opportunity to save money elsewhere,” said Paul McAdam, senior director of banking and payments intelligence at JD Power.

“When household budgets are tight, a monthly banking fee becomes an expense worth reconsidering.”

RBC ranked highest among the Big 5 for a third straight year at 619. BMO and CIBC tied for second at 611, with TD close behind in fourth at 610.

Among midsize banks, Tangerine Bank took the top spot for a 15th consecutive year at 676, followed by ATB Financial at 650.

Why are younger bank customers ready to leave?

The findings echo an Equifax Canada survey showing most mortgage holders would consider switching lenders at renewal. Tracy Valko, founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, described the financial strain behind that restlessness at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

“One out of two Canadians are $200 away from not meeting their financial obligations every month. And that’s profound. We never had this before. And they need that empathy – to see as a mortgage broker that you care about that,” she said.

The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) says frontier AI is among the fastest-growing threats facing lenders, warning that advanced models can help adversaries identify and exploit vulnerabilities at greater speed and scale. https://t.co/B9plArK6ju — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 12, 2026

What the bank switching trend means for mortgage brokers

A client willing to leave a bank over a monthly fee is a client willing to shop at renewal. Valko, who joined MortgageFest Canada’s Day 1 panel on the path forward for brokers, said winning that client takes more than price.

“As an industry, we got away from where it was about transactions and how many deals you did. Now it’s about focusing on that financial plan and strategy for that client, building that long-term financial relationship. So you look like a true expert and not just a rate agent.”

Prakash Bector, vice-president of national sales and distribution at EQ Bank, sees the opening.

"It's just staying focused on what we have in our control. So from a broker standpoint, it's those consistent outreaches to clients, leveraging your database, building new referral sources," she said during the mortgage event.

“As challenging as the market is, there’s immense opportunity for brokers. I think brokers’ share will continue to grow. A lot of clients need sound advice right now – they’re struggling, they don’t know what’s going to happen next. And this is where brokers play a critical role.”

Technology is part of that pitch, though not as advice. Fraud prevention and data security topped customers’ preferred uses of bank AI at 31%, against 12% for personal financial advice, a useful signal for brokers weighing how mortgage professionals can keep up with AI.

JD Power surveyed 14,038 retail banking customers in two waves during 2026.

items.title: Royal LePage: trade tensions stall Canada’s fall housing market
items.description: Rate hike fears and tariffs keep buyers waiting as brokers head into a slower autumn
items.content: <p>Rate hike fears and tariffs keep buyers waiting as brokers head into a slower autumn</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/073/0388_639276754438511603.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Rate hike fears and tariffs keep buyers waiting as brokers head into a slower autumn
items.body:
Canada’s housing market stalled in the third quarter of 2026 as new US tariffs and the prospect of higher mortgage rates kept buyers sidelined, according to the Royal LePage House Price Survey and Market Forecast.

The national aggregate home price slipped 0.8% year over year to $810,000 and fell 0.6% from the second quarter. Royal LePage now forecasts a 1.0% annual gain in the fourth quarter, down from the 2.0% it projected in its second-quarter house price survey.

Greater Toronto Area prices fell 3.7% to $1,073,100, while Greater Vancouver dropped 4.0% to $1,148,100.

Greater Montreal bucked the trend with a 2.9% gain to $653,700, and Prairie markets held steadier.

The trade dispute escalated after talks collapsed on Aug. 21 and Washington imposed a 50% tariff on a wide range of Canadian goods a day later.

“For many buyers, the hesitation is less about what they can afford today than how secure they feel about tomorrow,” said Phil Soper, president and CEO of Royal LePage.

“Buyers have more negotiating power, but little control over the forces shaping their confidence.”

BMO senior economist Sal Guatieri flagged the same risk in April.

“Unfortunately, it’s the economic uncertainty – both related to the trade war and the Iran war – that will likely keep a lot of buyers, especially first-time buyers, on the sidelines,” he said.

Royal LePage home prices by market, Q3 2026

Aggregate and median prices, with Royal LePage’s year-end forecast

*Forecast change in aggregate price, Q4 2026 vs. Q4 2025. Prices include resale and new build. Negative figures shown in red.
Source: Royal LePage House Price Survey and Market Forecast, Q3 2026 (released Oct. 15, 2026); price data from RPS Real Property Solutions

Mortgage rate jitters fail to pull buyers forward

The Bank of Canada has held its overnight rate at 2.25% for a year, with announcements due Oct. 28 and Dec. 9. Soper expects a hold through 2026 and a hike in early 2027, though a growing number of forecasters are calling for an October rate hike.

Yet the threat of costlier borrowing has not created urgency. “Low confidence is outweighing the urgency to lock in today’s favourable borrowing costs,” Soper said.

Renewals add another layer of pressure. The Royal LePage 2026 Mortgage Renewal Survey found 38% of mortgage holders expect higher payments at renewal.

Grant Armstrong, chief growth officer at WealthOne Bank of Canada, is among those expecting an earlier move.

“I think rates will probably go up in October. GIC rates are up 35 points in the last sixty to ninety days. Bank of Canada bond rates are up 60 points. Like everything’s been going up already. So it’s just a natural part of the market,” he shared during MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

Yet the threat of costlier borrowing has not created urgency. “Low confidence is outweighing the urgency to lock in today’s favourable borrowing costs,” Soper said.

Renewals add another layer of pressure. The Royal LePage 2026 Mortgage Renewal Survey found 38% of mortgage holders expect higher payments at renewal. Armstrong argued the risk is manageable.

“I think everyone got really worried about the renewal cliff. So they got really good at preparing for it. And I think that preparation has taken the noise out of it,” he said.

“We’re in normal rates today. We’re not in obscenely high rates. So I think the renewal cliff doesn’t exist to the extreme, but it’s something we need to be aware of.”

Don Kottick of RE/MAX Canada says buyers remain willing to make compromises, from relocating farther from city centres to adjusting their spending habits, to achieve their homeownership goals. https://t.co/GOHrsHlsWY — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 14, 2026

What brokers are seeing on the ground

For buyers who do act, leverage has shifted. “Conditions of finance are back in. Home inspections, everything, you name it. Water testing. We have price reductions,” said Sarita Free, a mortgage agent with Mortgage Powered Financial Group in Norfolk County, Ont., who spoke at MortgageFest.

Tracy Valko, founder of AIMI Mortgage Collective, said brokers must understand the macro picture without guessing at it.

“There’s a lot of global tensions right now that are affecting our market. What’s affecting bond yields? What affects fixed rates? Agents and brokers should know that. We as mortgage agents and brokers should never predict, but one thing we should do is make sure that we understand the knowledge so we can future-prepare homeowners for what could be coming down the pipeline,” she explained during the mortgage event.

Andy Kuyper, head of partnerships and secured lending at TransUnion, sees a slow climb rather than a rebound and also shared his thoughts during MortgageFest Canada.

“I’d like to be optimistic. I think we’re facing the reality that with the geopolitical climate and everything that’s happening here, our mortgage industry is probably not ready to rebound. We are seeing slight growth in originations, we’re seeing slight growth in mortgage balances – a lot more on the refi side,” he said.

Soper remains measured. “Canada’s housing market is on a detour, not a derailment,” he said.

items.title: How credit unions are navigating a turbulent 2026 market
items.description: CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility
items.content: <p>CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639276728476168839.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: CEO spells out careful approach in a lending environment marked by risk and plenty of volatility
items.body:
Canada’s current housing market is moribund, according to a leading community lending chief executive officer. And that means credit unions are navigating a difficult balancing act: maintaining volumes without taking on undue risk in a market where prices are still falling.

Fausto Gaudio, president and chief executive officer of the Toronto-headquartered IC Savings, described the current market as one where activity was barely getting off the ground. “It’s very, very soft,” he told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “Softer than it was last year – and last year was also a very soft year in terms of trades and prices declining as well.”

That marks one of the biggest obstacles facing credit unions and other lenders. Maintaining asset size is no easy feat, but loosening credit standards to bring more business in isn’t always the best idea either as values continue to slide.

“Top of mind is that there just isn’t enough volume,” Gaudio said. “It’s very, very difficult… to maintain asset size, because unless we expand our risk tolerance and do mortgages at a higher loan-to-value at a time when prices are declining. That’s a real challenge, especially for small boutique lenders.”

Gaudio said IC Savings has opted to hold its position rather than chase volume, steering clear of high-LTV lending. “We do very few mortgages at the 80% loan-to-value,” he said. “And so we don’t seem to have a lot of the problems that the big banks have in terms of defaults and powers of sale today.”

But there’s also opportunity in the market, not least in serving borrowers who fall outside standard bank approval criteria. Tighter lending standards among Canada’s banking giants mean borrowers often don’t qualify in the current market not because of recklessness, but rather circumstance.

When dealing with those customers, understanding the story – and the “why” of how their current situation developed – is crucial, according to Gaudio.

“With somebody that might have had a difficulty – having gone through a health problem, a period of unemployment, a marital breakup – we’re much more attentive to those human stories and try to resolve their problems,” he said.

“When a borrower is coming out of a life experience and a setback, we’re much more willing to try to resolve their issue – but at the same time, they need to have some equity to offset that risk.”

Reverse mortgages: Will their popularity grow in the credit union space?

Gaudio said IC Savings has developed a new term reverse mortgage, a fixed-period alternative to the traditional lifetime arrangement, aimed at homeowners who want to access equity but have a clear exit plan within a few years.

The product, he said, is for “someone that wants to live in their house another three or possibly five years, but then they have a plan – to move back to Northern Ontario or the East Coast where they had family or grandkids – but they don’t want to commit to a reverse mortgage for life.”

2027 outlook for wider market remains unclear

Gaudio sees the current housing market sluggishness as a product of rampant unaffordability rather than the geopolitical headwinds hovering over the Canadian economy.

Trade turmoil and rising oil prices, he said, have less impact of the housing market than the fact that prices have skyrocketed over the past decade, and remain elevated in many regions despite the years-long cooldown.

It remains unclear whether the broader market will normalize quickly enough to ease volume pressure on boutique lenders heading into 2027, but with borrower stress likely to continue rising, he emphasized the importance of brokers and agents telling their customer’s story in as much detail as possible to boost their chances of getting a deal through.

“I believe the brokers that deal with us know us as that type of lender,” he said.

items.title: Housing coalition outlines four demands ahead of B.C. election
items.description: Developers and affordable housing providers urge parties to restore planned investments and reduce development costs
items._ogDesc: Developers and affordable housing providers urge parties to restore planned investments and reduce development costs
items.body:
Market-rate developers and non-profit housing providers are joining forces to urge B.C.’s political parties to reduce the cost of building homes, warning that rising expenses and policy uncertainty are leaving projects stalled.

The Urban Development Institute (UDI), B.C. Non-Profit Housing Association (BCNPHA), Aboriginal Housing Management Association (AHMA) and Co-operative Housing Federation of B.C. (CHF BC) on Tuesday called on all parties to commit to four measures aimed at making housing development more financially viable.

The groups said the cost of building and financing homes in B.C. has exceeded what many buyers can afford and what governments are willing to subsidize for low- and moderate-income renters, resulting in projects failing to get off the drawing board.

“When market developers and non-profit housing providers are asking for the same thing, it should tell every party how serious the cost of delivery crisis is,” said Mike Drummond, CEO of UDI, in a statement.

The groups are asking the next provincial government to restore planned investments in non-profit, co-operative and Indigenous housing, allowing more than 5,000 affordable rental homes that were deferred following $1.4 billion in recent budget cuts to proceed.

“The projects are ready, but the land sits empty,” said Jill Atkey, CEO of the B.C. Non-Profit Housing Association.

“The people waiting for affordable housing cannot wait another budget cycle. The next government has an opportunity to restore the investment and get these homes built.”

The coalition also called on the government to co-invest remaining BC Rental Protection Funds with the Canada Rental Protection Fund to “continue protecting the affordability that already exists in the market.”

In addition, the groups urged the next government to finalize a federal-provincial agreement to reduce development cost charges and fund infrastructure needed to support new housing within 90 days of forming government.

The federal and provincial governments announced a 10-year partnership in June under which they would each contribute nearly $1.6 billion to reduce development charges for multi-unit housing by up to 50 per cent in priority communities and fund infrastructure.

“The details were not finalized before the election was called, so builders cannot price it into projects and municipalities cannot act on it,” said the coalition in a statement Tuesday.

Lastly, the groups called for a federal GST exemption on new homes for all eligible buyers rather than limiting relief to first-time purchasers. They pointed to Ontario’s expanded HST rebate program, announced in March, which temporarily eliminated the 13 per cent HST on eligible buyers of new homes valued at $1 million or less.

“The commitments made in 2024 need to translate into homes on the ground,” said Margaret Pfoh, CEO of the Aboriginal Housing Management Association, in a statement.

items._ogDesc: Canadians expect to buy their first home at 41, while nearly half of homeowners can’t afford their next move, an RBC poll finds.
items.body:
Canada’s housing ladder isn’t just hard to get on—nearly half of owners can’t afford to get off the first rung. RBC’s 2026 Home Ownership Poll looked at home buying expectations and financial constraints. The poll shows first-time buyers are getting older, and fewer owners can afford to upgrade. Meanwhile, the Bank of Mom and Dad is expanding its territory—literally, as multi-generational living returns.

Canada’s First-Time Buyers Expect To Buy Their First Home At 41

Canada’s first-time buyers will be on the back half of life’s golf course before they get into the market. Aspiring first-time owners plan to buy at 41 years old on average, 12 years later than current owners. That may be an optimistic number, as nearly half of them were unsure when they would be able to buy a home.

Becoming a homeowner is much harder than it was for past generations, said most (74%) of non-owners. Over 3 in 4 (77%) believe buying is harder than it was in the past, and 60% say traditional buyer advice is no longer true. Existing homeowners are likely to agree with that last point.

Canadian Homeowners Can’t Afford To Upgrade Their Starter Home

High home prices don’t just impact first-time buyers, it causes buyer gridlock. Modern housing markets are built around the concept of a property ladder. Homebuyers progressively move up the ladder, upgrading as they build equity. That process has been breaking down, as fewer people can afford to upgrade.

Nearly half (46%) of current owners want a larger or different home, but say it’s not financially realistic. Most (52%) say moving up from their first home is harder than expected, a problem the whole industry is about to feel. If existing starter home owners can’t buy the next rung, those sellers face reduced liquidity. At the same time, there are fewer starter homes for buyers to get onto the property ladder in the first place.

Aspiring first-time homebuyers are taking note and skipping the ladder. The survey found 74% are looking for a long-term home instead of a starter. Starting ownership 12 years later than average means very different property needs. Delaying their buy until the age of their peak earnings growth can help them afford to skip the starter. It also means starter homeowners will see their liquidity turn into their competition.

RBC senior mortgage specialist Brad Evjen suggests this may not always be the best strategy. “Buying a home you can stay in longer usually means stretching your budget further, so the math has to work in both directions,” he notes. He prefers to walk clients through monthly payments against what moving up in five years would cost.

Usually, the down payment problem is a bigger hurdle than the monthly payment. First-time buyers are increasingly tapping the Bank of Mom and Dad. However, not everyone’s parents are rich—some are actually looking for help with their own cost of living.

Multi-Generational Households Return With High Home Prices

Canada’s lack of affordability may soon reverse nuclear households to their pre-war roots. The survey found that 57% of prospective first-time buyers would consider multi-generational living—parents living with their adult children. However, it’s not just a first-time buyer thing—most buyers (53%), including those who currently own, would consider multi-generational living. Nearly half (44%) of all respondents, including those not in the housing market at all, would also consider the option.

Only a few years ago, it became normal for parents to help with a down payment. Now 29% of prospective first-time buyers say multi-generational buying is more a necessity than a choice. A problem that parents are receptive to—35% of homeowners say they’re prepared to sell and jointly buy with their kids to help them enter the market.

Canada’s housing ladder is difficult to enter—and getting onto it doesn’t guarantee you can climb it. Those looking to enter the market can’t do so until much later in life. At the same time, those who own are increasingly struggling to upgrade from their starter. Helping to bridge the gap are families pooling resources to buy what was considered normal for the last three generations.

items.title: OCC debanking report names TD Bank, BMO in major US probe
items.description: US debanking probe names TD Bank and BMO among nine lenders, with implications for Canadian brokers
items.content: <p>US debanking probe names TD Bank and BMO among nine lenders, with implications for Canadian brokers</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639276064635054189.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: US debanking probe names TD Bank and BMO among nine lenders, with implications for Canadian brokers
items.body:
Two of Canada’s largest lenders, Toronto-Dominion Bank (TD) and the Bank of Montreal (BMO), are among nine institutions named in a new US debanking report — one that found major banks had denied financial services to customers based on their political beliefs or lawful business activities.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) launched its supervisory review in September 2025 following a presidential executive order titled “Guaranteeing Fair Access to Banking for All Americans.”

The review examined nearly 100,000 complaints and approximately 420,000 pages of documents from all nine banks — JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, Capital One, and PNC Bank, alongside TD Bank and BMO — and found that all had maintained policies limiting customer access on non-financial grounds at some point between 2020 and September 2025.

Broad reputation risk policies under review

Jonathan V. Gould, Comptroller of the Currency in Washington, described the findings as “irrefutable evidence” that these banks had “denied, debanked and discriminated against customers and lawful businesses.”

He added: “Fair access to financial services is not a mantra — it is a mandate.”

The OCC found that broad, poorly defined reputation risk policies, or those lacking objective and risk-based criteria, were used to restrict client access across sectors including oil and gas exploration, coal mining, firearms and ammunition manufacturing, tobacco and e-cigarette distribution, detention facility operations, and digital assets.

Implications for the broker channel

The OCC’s findings carry immediate weight for Canadian mortgage brokers, for whom both TD and BMO are significant lender partners.

TD Bank, which has moved to sell approximately US$9 billion in US mortgage holdings to comply with an asset cap imposed after its US$3.1 billion anti-money laundering settlement, remains a major broker channel lender in Canada.

According to Canadian Mortgage Professional’s coverage of MortgageFest Canada, Devon Ajram, vice-president, broker services and operations at TD Bank in Toronto, disclosed that close to 50% of the customers TD gains through the broker channel are new to the bank, a measure of just how critical that channel is to the lender’s growth.

BMO, which has been growing its broker presence through its BrokerEdge platform, is also an expanding partner in the channel. Brokers with clients in energy, firearms retail, or digital assets should note that these sectors featured prominently in the OCC’s findings — and as CMP’s earlier reporting on big bank CEO outlooks found, US policy shifts at these lenders have a habit of crossing the border.

Comptroller Gould acknowledged that while some banks had begun moderating these practices, he was “not confident” these steps would be enough. The OCC has signalled it will consider further changes to its regulatory framework for the largest banks.
